name: Education & Learning Sciences
tagline: From curiosity and practice to teaching, assessment and learning research.

nodes.title: Look, Listen and Wonder
nodes.goal: Notice a feature, ask a question and explore with adult support.
learning_outcomes: Describe or indicate an observable feature.
Ask a question about a familiar object.
Choose an adult-supported way to explore.

lesson.overview: Learning often begins with noticing. We can look closely, listen, touch safe objects and ask what we wonder about. An observation describes what we notice; a question asks something we do not yet know. Adults can help us choose safe ways to explore rather than guessing every answer immediately. Children can show their thinking with words, pointing, movement or drawings, so speech is not the only way to participate.
lesson.worked_example: A child notices that a dry sponge feels light and asks what happens when it gets wet. An adult helps add water in a tray, then the child compares the two states.
lesson.activity: Explore a safe familiar object with an adult. Point to or describe two features, ask one question, and draw what you noticed.
lesson.reflection: What did you notice that you had not noticed before?

quiz.prompt: You notice a leaf is green. What did you do?
quiz.explain: An observation describes something you notice.
quiz.say: You notice a leaf is green. What did you do?

quiz.prompt: Which asks a question?
quiz.explain: A question asks about something you want to know.
quiz.say: Which asks a question?

quiz.prompt: You find an unknown object outside. What is a safe next step?
quiz.explain: An adult can help decide how to explore safely.
quiz.say: You find an unknown object outside. What is a safe next step?

quiz.prompt: A child points instead of speaking. Can that show an idea?
quiz.explain: People can communicate by pointing and many other ways.
quiz.say: A child points instead of speaking. Can that show an idea?

quiz.prompt: You want to hear a quiet sound. What helps?
quiz.explain: Listening closely makes quiet details easier to notice.
quiz.say: You want to hear a quiet sound. What helps?

quiz.prompt: You do not know an answer yet. What can you do?
quiz.explain: Questions are a useful starting point for learning.
quiz.say: You do not know an answer yet. What can you do?

nodes.kid_text: Look, listen and wonder. What do you notice? You can point, talk or draw. A trusted grown-up can help you explore safely.

nodes.title: Trying, Practising and Asking for Help
nodes.goal: Use practice, feedback and help to improve a simple task.
learning_outcomes: Treat a mistake as information about an attempt.
Change one feature after feedback.
Ask for help or a break when needed.

lesson.overview: A new skill often takes several attempts. Each attempt gives us something to notice: what worked, what changed and where help would be useful. Practice is most useful when we pay attention and adjust rather than repeating a confusing action forever. Rest can help when we are tired or upset. Asking for help is part of learning, and a mistake describes an attempt, not a person’s worth.
lesson.worked_example: A block bridge falls. An adult asks the child to notice how far apart the supports are. The child moves them closer and tries again, then compares the two bridges.
lesson.activity: Build a small block bridge with support from an adult. Change one thing after a fall, describe the change, and take a break if needed.
lesson.reflection: What kind of help made your next try easier?

quiz.prompt: Your tower falls. What can help you learn?
choices: Look at why and try a change
quiz.answer: Look at why and try a change
quiz.explain: Noticing what happened can guide the next attempt.
quiz.say: Your tower falls. What can help you learn?

quiz.prompt: You feel very tired while practising. What may help?
quiz.explain: Rest can make it easier to pay attention again.
quiz.say: You feel very tired while practising. What may help?

quiz.prompt: You cannot tie a knot yet. What can you ask?
choices: Can you show me one step?
Can you say I am hopeless?
quiz.answer: Can you show me one step?
quiz.explain: A small demonstration can support learning.
quiz.say: You cannot tie a knot yet. What can you ask?

quiz.prompt: One attempt goes wrong. Does that make you a bad person?
quiz.explain: A mistake concerns an action, not your worth.
quiz.say: One attempt goes wrong. Does that make you a bad person?

quiz.prompt: Which feedback helps build a stronger bridge?
quiz.explain: Specific feedback suggests an action to test.
quiz.say: Which feedback helps build a stronger bridge?

quiz.prompt: After changing the bridge, what should you do?
quiz.explain: Comparing attempts helps you learn from the change.
quiz.say: After changing the bridge, what should you do?

nodes.kid_text: We learn by trying, noticing and trying again. A mistake does not make you bad. You can ask for one small step of help or take a rest.

nodes.title: Remembering and Explaining
nodes.goal: Practise recalling an idea and explaining it in your own words.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish recognition from recall.
Use retrieval followed by correction.
Explain an idea in personal words.

lesson.overview: Looking at an answer can make it feel familiar, but remembering it without looking asks us to retrieve it. We can practise with a question, check the answer, and correct mistakes. Returning to an idea after a gap gives another opportunity to remember. Explaining the idea in our own words can reveal what makes sense and what still needs help. These strategies work best with understandable material and supportive feedback, not with guessing endlessly at something never taught.
lesson.worked_example: After learning three parts of a plant, Sam covers the picture and names them. Sam forgets the stem, checks the picture, explains what it does, and tries again the next day.
lesson.activity: Learn three facts from a short passage. Close it, draw or say what you remember, then check and correct. Return to the facts tomorrow with an adult or partner.
lesson.reflection: Which felt easier: recognizing the answer or recalling it without looking?

quiz.prompt: Which action practises remembering?
choices: Close the page and recall the idea
quiz.answer: Close the page and recall the idea
quiz.explain: Recall asks you to retrieve the idea from memory.
quiz.say: Which action practises remembering?

quiz.prompt: You recall a fact incorrectly. Next you should?
quiz.explain: Feedback helps prevent practising an incorrect answer.
quiz.say: You recall a fact incorrectly. Next you should?

quiz.prompt: Why revisit a topic tomorrow?
choices: To practise remembering after a gap
quiz.answer: To practise remembering after a gap
quiz.explain: Spacing creates another opportunity to retrieve the idea.
quiz.say: Why revisit a topic tomorrow?

quiz.prompt: An answer looks familiar. Does that guarantee you can explain it?
quiz.explain: Familiarity can differ from usable understanding.
quiz.say: An answer looks familiar. Does that guarantee you can explain it?

quiz.prompt: A helpful explanation uses?
quiz.explain: Explaining meaning reveals what you understand.
quiz.say: A helpful explanation uses?

quiz.prompt: You never understood a new idea. What should come before repeated guessing?
quiz.explain: Practice needs something meaningful to learn and retrieve.
quiz.say: You never understood a new idea. What should come before repeated guessing?

nodes.kid_text: Try remembering a little without looking, then check. Explain it in your own words. Come back later and try again. Ask for help when the idea is not clear.

nodes.title: Teaching a Friend One Step at a Time
nodes.goal: Give clear instructions, check understanding and adapt support.
learning_outcomes: Sequence clear instructions.
Use a demonstration to support understanding.
Give specific and respectful feedback.

lesson.overview: Teaching means helping someone learn, so we start by finding out what the learner already knows. Clear instructions break a task into manageable steps and show an example when useful. A learner may need more time, a picture or a different explanation. Checking understanding means asking the learner to show or explain, rather than assuming a nod means everything is clear. Helpful feedback describes an action and a next step respectfully.
lesson.worked_example: A child teaches a friend to fold a paper boat. Instead of giving all instructions at once, the child demonstrates one fold, asks the friend to try, then checks whether the corners line up.
lesson.activity: Teach a partner a safe three-step drawing or folding task. Ask what they know first, demonstrate, and revise one instruction based on what they show you.
lesson.reflection: How did your partner’s attempt help you improve your explanation?

quiz.prompt: Before teaching a task, it helps to ask?
quiz.explain: Prior knowledge helps choose the right starting point.
quiz.say: Before teaching a task, it helps to ask?

quiz.prompt: A learner looks confused after many instructions. What may help?
quiz.explain: Breaking the task down can reduce confusion.
quiz.say: A learner looks confused after many instructions. What may help?

quiz.prompt: Which checks understanding?
choices: You nodded, so you know everything
quiz.explain: A demonstration gives evidence of what the learner can do.
quiz.say: Which checks understanding?

quiz.prompt: Which feedback is useful?
choices: You are just bad at this
quiz.explain: Specific feedback names an action the learner can change.
quiz.say: Which feedback is useful?

quiz.prompt: Your friend needs more time. What can you do?
quiz.explain: Learners can need different amounts of time and support.
quiz.say: Your friend needs more time. What can you do?

quiz.prompt: Your instructions did not work. What can change?
quiz.explain: Teachers can adapt their approach based on evidence.
quiz.say: Your instructions did not work. What can change?

nodes.kid_text: Teach one small step. Show it, let your friend try, and listen. Kind, clear feedback tells someone what to change next.

nodes.title: Planning and Checking Your Learning
nodes.goal: Set a specific learning goal and adjust a study plan using evidence.
learning_outcomes: Write an observable learning goal.
Compare confidence with task performance.
Revise a study strategy from evidence.

lesson.overview: Self-regulated learning connects planning, practice and reflection. A specific goal describes what you want to be able to do, such as explain why fractions need a common unit before addition. A study plan chooses actions that match that goal and leaves time to check progress. Confidence is useful information but can be misleading, so compare it with an actual attempt. Reflection then identifies an effective strategy, a remaining gap and a concrete adjustment.
lesson.worked_example: Lea feels ready for a fractions quiz after rereading. A short practice question reveals confusion about denominators. Lea studies a worked example, solves a similar problem, and checks again instead of simply rereading every page.
lesson.activity: Choose a small topic and write a performance goal. Predict how well you can do, attempt a task without help, compare the result with your prediction, and revise tomorrow’s plan.
lesson.reflection: What evidence would show that your plan is working?

quiz.prompt: Which goal is most specific?
choices: Become better at school in general
Spend a long time studying science
quiz.explain: A specific goal names an observable performance.

quiz.prompt: Feeling fluent while rereading proves mastery?
quiz.explain: Recognition can overstate what you can produce unaided.

quiz.prompt: A plan should change when?
choices: When a timer ends regardless of results
When evidence shows a learning gap
quiz.answer: When evidence shows a learning gap
quiz.explain: Monitoring informs useful adjustments.

quiz.prompt: Which activity best checks explanation skill?
choices: Explain the idea without the text
quiz.answer: Explain the idea without the text
quiz.explain: The check should match the intended learning performance.

quiz.prompt: A reflection says “I am stupid.” What is missing?
choices: A specific process and next step
quiz.answer: A specific process and next step
quiz.explain: Useful reflection identifies changeable strategies and knowledge gaps.

quiz.prompt: Your prediction is high but performance low. This suggests?
choices: The task result should be ignored
quiz.explain: Comparing prediction and evidence helps improve self-monitoring.

quiz.prompt: You solve familiar examples but fail a new context. Your next goal should target?
choices: Apply the principle in varied contexts
Count the pages in the chapter again
quiz.answer: Apply the principle in varied contexts
quiz.explain: The evidence reveals a transfer gap.

quiz.prompt: A plan leaves no time to check errors. What is missing?
choices: More notes with the same content
quiz.explain: Checking supports correction and better planning.

quiz.prompt: A student predicts 9/10 but scores 4/10 repeatedly. A useful adjustment is?
choices: Use confidence as the final score
quiz.explain: Monitoring can align confidence with demonstrated performance.

quiz.prompt: Which record best supports reflection?
quiz.explain: Specific evidence connects practice with improvement.

quiz.prompt: You feel ready after rereading but cannot explain the idea without notes. Write a revised study plan.
quiz.answer: Set an explanation goal, attempt retrieval without notes and check the gaps with feedback. Practise a new example and use the next independent attempt to revise the plan.
quiz.explain: Set an explanation goal, attempt retrieval without notes and check the gaps with feedback. Practise a new example and use the next independent attempt to revise the plan.

nodes.title: Different Learners, Accessible Lessons
nodes.goal: Adapt learning materials to reduce barriers while preserving the learning goal.
learning_outcomes: Identify a barrier in a learning task.
Choose a support matched to that barrier.
Preserve the intended learning goal while adapting access.

lesson.overview: Learners differ in experience, language, sensory access and available tools. An accessible lesson makes the goal clear and offers suitable ways to encounter information and show understanding. A diagram may need a spoken or written description; a spoken explanation may need captions or text. These supports should respond to an actual barrier, rather than assigning every learner a fixed “type.” The same person may benefit from different representations for different tasks.
lesson.worked_example: A lesson aims to explain the water cycle. A student cannot access an unlabelled animation, so the teacher adds a labelled still diagram and a text description. The science goal stays the same while the access route improves.
lesson.activity: Review a short fictional lesson for barriers involving vision, hearing, language and motor access. Redesign two features and explain how each change supports the stated goal.
lesson.reflection: How can you check with a learner whether a support is useful?

quiz.prompt: A video contains essential speech. What supports a learner who cannot hear it?
quiz.explain: Text can provide access to the spoken information.

quiz.prompt: A chart uses only red and green to distinguish groups. A useful change is?
quiz.explain: Multiple cues reduce dependence on colour alone.

quiz.prompt: Should every learner be assigned one permanent learning style?
choices: No, match support to task and barrier
Yes, let a permanent label decide
quiz.answer: No, match support to task and barrier
quiz.explain: Needs and useful representations vary by task and context.

quiz.prompt: An adaptation should preserve?
quiz.explain: Access can change without removing the core intellectual task.

quiz.prompt: Why ask learners about a support?
choices: They can describe the actual barrier
quiz.answer: They can describe the actual barrier
quiz.explain: User feedback helps evaluate accessibility in practice.

quiz.prompt: A text uses unfamiliar words. A useful support is?
quiz.explain: Vocabulary support can make the same content more accessible.

quiz.prompt: A learner cannot use a mouse accurately. A relevant support is?
quiz.explain: Alternative input can reduce a motor-access barrier.

quiz.prompt: A science diagram has no description. A text alternative should?
choices: Repeat its file name as description
quiz.explain: Meaningful alternatives convey the diagram’s instructional content.

quiz.prompt: A teacher offers several ways to explain a concept. The common requirement should be?
quiz.explain: Response modes can differ while the learning criterion remains.

quiz.prompt: A support helps one task but confuses another. What follows?
quiz.explain: Effectiveness depends on the barrier and goal.

quiz.prompt: A lesson’s essential information appears in a colour-only chart. Propose an adaptation that preserves the learning goal.
quiz.answer: Add clear labels or patterns and a text description of the relationships. This improves access while keeping the same concept and reasoning goal.
quiz.explain: Add clear labels or patterns and a text description of the relationships. This improves access while keeping the same concept and reasoning goal.

nodes.title: Designing Lessons and Assessments
nodes.goal: Align learning objectives, teaching activities and assessment evidence.
learning_outcomes: Write an assessable objective.
Align activities and evidence with the objective.
Distinguish formative from summative uses of assessment.

lesson.overview: Lesson design begins by deciding what learners should know or be able to do. Activities then provide opportunities to develop that performance, and assessments gather evidence of it. Misalignment occurs when, for example, a course promises argument evaluation but tests only names and dates. Formative assessment is used during learning to guide next steps; summative assessment summarizes achievement for a stated purpose. Both depend on tasks that reveal the intended understanding and on feedback learners can act on.
lesson.worked_example: A lesson goal is to compare two explanations for a historical event. Memorizing the authors’ names is insufficient evidence. A short written comparison using evidence better matches the goal, while a midpoint discussion can reveal misconceptions before final submission.
lesson.activity: Design a 20-minute lesson with one objective, two learning activities, one formative check and a final evidence task. Explain how each component connects to the objective.
lesson.reflection: Could a learner succeed at your assessment without understanding the intended idea?

quiz.prompt: A goal asks learners to evaluate evidence. Best assessment?
quiz.explain: The task should require the intended reasoning.

quiz.prompt: Assessment is formative when results are used to?
quiz.explain: Its formative function depends on how evidence is used.

quiz.prompt: A final examination is commonly used to?
quiz.explain: Summative assessment serves a reporting purpose with limits.

quiz.prompt: Which objective is assessable?
choices: Justify a choice with two reasons
Become excellent in a broad sense
quiz.answer: Justify a choice with two reasons
quiz.explain: Observable performance makes evidence requirements clearer.

quiz.prompt: Feedback is actionable when it?
choices: Names a gap and feasible action
quiz.answer: Names a gap and feasible action
quiz.explain: Learners need information they can use to improve.

quiz.prompt: A beautifully produced poster may hide weak reasoning if?
quiz.explain: Assessment criteria can drift away from the intended construct.

quiz.prompt: Students must defend a claim, but class time is spent copying definitions. What needs revision?
quiz.explain: Learning opportunities should develop the assessed performance.

quiz.prompt: A midpoint question reveals the same misconception in many learners. The teacher should?
choices: Wait for final grades before responding
Treat the check as unrelated to teaching
quiz.explain: Formative evidence becomes useful when acted on.

quiz.prompt: A rubric says “excellent” without criteria. What is missing?
choices: A larger number of score levels
quiz.explain: Criteria should make quality interpretable.

quiz.prompt: A task tests teamwork but assigns one shared score. Which inference is limited?
choices: The existence of the group product
quiz.explain: A group score may not distinguish individual performance.

quiz.prompt: A course promises evidence evaluation but tests only dates. Explain how you would realign it.
quiz.answer: The objective requires reasoning about evidence. Add practice comparing claims and use an assessment that asks learners to justify a conclusion, with feedback during learning.
quiz.explain: The objective requires reasoning about evidence. Add practice comparing claims and use an assessment that asks learners to justify a conclusion, with feedback during learning.

nodes.title: Learning, Memory and Transfer
nodes.goal: Use learning-science concepts to explain practice, feedback and transfer limits.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish immediate performance from learning.
Explain how examples and practice can support novices.
Design a task that checks transfer.

lesson.overview: Learning is a lasting change in knowledge or capability, while performance is what a person shows at a particular moment. Easy practice can produce fluent immediate performance without strong later recall. Worked examples can support novices by making steps visible, and practice can gradually require more independent decisions. Transfer means using learning in a new situation; it often requires recognizing the underlying structure beneath changed surface details. Evidence about an average effect does not imply that one strategy suits every learner, content area or stage of expertise.
lesson.worked_example: A student solves area problems after seeing rectangles in one orientation. A rotated rectangle causes difficulty even though the rule is unchanged. Comparing both diagrams and explaining base and height can help connect the shared structure.
lesson.activity: Create two problems with the same underlying principle but different surface contexts. Teach the principle, plan spaced retrieval with feedback, and specify a delayed transfer task.
lesson.reflection: How would you distinguish short-term fluency from durable understanding?

quiz.prompt: Strong performance immediately after copying an example proves?
quiz.explain: A later independent task is needed to assess retention and transfer.

quiz.prompt: Worked examples can help novices by?
quiz.explain: Examples can reduce demands while learners build knowledge.

quiz.prompt: A transfer task changes?
choices: The answer without a new problem
Ink colour without a new demand
quiz.explain: Transfer asks learners to recognize and apply knowledge beyond practice conditions.

quiz.prompt: Too much unrelated decoration can hinder learning by?
quiz.explain: Extraneous demands can distract from the target material.

quiz.prompt: A delayed test is useful for checking?
quiz.explain: Delay helps distinguish durable recall from momentary fluency.

quiz.prompt: A study finds an average benefit from a strategy. It implies?
choices: Evidence that other methods are useless
A finding within the study’s scope
A guarantee across learners and tasks
quiz.answer: A finding within the study’s scope
quiz.explain: Effects can vary with learners, materials and implementation.

quiz.prompt: A learner explains a principle in two contexts. Compared with one copied example, this gives more evidence of?
quiz.explain: Different contexts can reveal recognition of underlying structure.

quiz.prompt: An expert finds beginner examples repetitive. Teaching may need adjustment because?
quiz.explain: Expertise influences the demands and benefits of instructional supports.

quiz.prompt: Practice is distributed across several days. The design changes?
choices: The physical size of study materials
quiz.explain: Spacing concerns when practice occurs.

nodes.title: Assessment Validity and Measurement
nodes.goal: Evaluate assessment interpretations using validity, reliability and fairness evidence.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish validity from reliability.
Identify construct underrepresentation and irrelevant demands.
Develop evidence requirements for a score use.

lesson.overview: Assessment scores are observations used to support interpretations and decisions. Validity concerns the evidence and reasoning supporting a particular interpretation for a particular use; it is not a permanent stamp on a test. Reliability concerns consistency under specified conditions, and reliable scores can still measure the wrong thing. Construct underrepresentation occurs when important parts of the target are absent; construct-irrelevant variation occurs when unrelated demands influence scores. Fairness analysis examines access, consequences and whether comparable interpretations are justified across groups.
lesson.worked_example: A science test claims to measure causal reasoning but requires unusually difficult vocabulary. Language difficulty may introduce construct-irrelevant variation. Making wording accessible can improve the inference, provided the scientific reasoning demand remains.
lesson.activity: Create an assessment blueprint for one learning construct. Map tasks to dimensions, propose scoring criteria, examine a potential fairness issue and specify evidence needed before a high-stakes use.
lesson.reflection: Which interpretation of your score would be unjustified even if scorers agreed perfectly?

quiz.prompt: A test produces consistent scores but measures memorization instead of reasoning. It may be?
choices: Reliable but misaligned with the claim
quiz.answer: Reliable but misaligned with the claim
quiz.explain: Consistency does not establish that the intended construct is measured.

quiz.prompt: Validity concerns?
choices: Evidence for an interpretation and use
quiz.answer: Evidence for an interpretation and use
quiz.explain: Different uses can require different supporting evidence.

quiz.prompt: An assessment omits half the intended skill domain. This is?
quiz.explain: Important parts of the construct are missing.

quiz.prompt: Complex reading obscures a non-language target skill. This may be?
quiz.explain: Unrelated language demands can influence the score.

quiz.prompt: Agreement between two scorers mainly supports?
quiz.explain: Rater agreement is one part of reliability evidence.

quiz.prompt: Before using a score for a new purpose, researchers should?
choices: Evaluate evidence for the new use
quiz.answer: Evaluate evidence for the new use
quiz.explain: Interpretation and decision context determine the required validity argument.

quiz.prompt: A writing rubric rewards handwriting heavily although the goal is argument quality. Concern?
quiz.explain: Handwriting may influence scores beyond the intended construct.

quiz.prompt: Two raters agree perfectly on a flawed rubric. What can still be weak?
choices: The consistency of the shared rule
quiz.explain: Reliability does not resolve validity concerns.

quiz.prompt: A test predicts performance in one course. Using it for employment selection requires?
quiz.explain: New decisions can require different validity evidence.

quiz.prompt: A score difference shrinks after accessible formatting. Investigate?
quiz.explain: Format can create construct-irrelevant differences in access.

quiz.prompt: Two raters agree perfectly on a science test that mostly rewards difficult vocabulary. Evaluate the score’s use as evidence of scientific reasoning.
quiz.answer: Rater agreement supports reliability, but vocabulary may introduce construct-irrelevant variation. Validity for scientific reasoning requires evidence that the score reflects that construct rather than language difficulty.
quiz.explain: Rater agreement supports reliability, but vocabulary may introduce construct-irrelevant variation. Validity for scientific reasoning requires evidence that the score reflects that construct rather than language difficulty.

nodes.title: Educational Research and Evidence
nodes.goal: Design a study of teaching that addresses comparison, context and ethics.
learning_outcomes: Match a method to an educational question.
Identify clustering and implementation effects.
Plan ethical handling of learner data.

lesson.overview: Educational research asks what happens, how learning unfolds and under what conditions teaching approaches help. Randomized comparisons can support causal claims, while interviews and observations can reveal processes and experiences. Classrooms create dependence because learners share teachers and environments, so assignment and analysis levels matter. Consent, privacy, equitable participation and the possibility of withholding useful support require careful planning. Evidence is strongest when the method matches the question and the report distinguishes findings, interpretation and uncertainty.
lesson.worked_example: A school randomizes classrooms to two feedback approaches. Pupils within the same classroom are not independent replicas of the treatment assignment. The design needs enough classrooms, attention to teacher effects and analysis that accounts for clustering.
lesson.activity: Draft a fictional classroom study with a research question, assignment unit, outcome, comparison, consent approach and analysis limitations. Add interviews to investigate one mechanism and explain their role.
lesson.reflection: What can your chosen design answer well, and what would require a different method?

quiz.prompt: Classes are randomized but pupils share teachers. Analysis should consider?
quiz.explain: Shared conditions can correlate outcomes within classes.

quiz.prompt: Interviews are especially useful for studying?
choices: Exact prevalence without a sampling plan
quiz.explain: They provide contextual accounts with their own limitations.

quiz.prompt: A study changes both teacher and curriculum between groups. Concern?
quiz.explain: Multiple differences make attribution difficult.

quiz.prompt: Learner data should be collected?
quiz.explain: Educational purpose does not remove privacy and ethical obligations.

quiz.prompt: A comparison group helps estimate?
quiz.explain: It supports a counterfactual comparison under assumptions.

quiz.prompt: Implementation records explain?
choices: Why assignment need not be documented
quiz.explain: Delivery evidence helps interpret an intervention’s observed effects.

quiz.prompt: Only two classes are randomized, one to each condition. A key limitation is?
choices: No need to consider teacher differences
quiz.explain: Pupil numbers do not replace independent classroom replication.

quiz.prompt: A teacher changes the intervention halfway through. The study needs?
choices: Removal of changes from the report
quiz.explain: Implementation changes affect what was tested.

quiz.prompt: Students who struggle are more likely to miss the final test. This may create?
quiz.explain: Missingness related to outcomes can distort estimates.

quiz.prompt: An interview study seeks varied experiences. A defensible sampling plan might?
choices: Choose cases to confirm desired themes
quiz.explain: Purposive sampling can suit qualitative aims when its logic is explicit.

quiz.prompt: A study assigns one classroom to each teaching method and counts every pupil as an independent replication. Critique the design.
quiz.answer: Assignment occurs at the classroom level, so clustering and teacher differences matter. Many pupils do not create many independent assignment units; the study needs more classroom replication and suitable analysis.
quiz.explain: Assignment occurs at the classroom level, so clustering and teacher differences matter. Many pupils do not create many independent assignment units; the study needs more classroom replication and suitable analysis.

nodes.title: Graduate Evidence Synthesis and Meta-analysis
nodes.goal: Plan and critique a systematic synthesis of educational evidence.
learning_outcomes: Create a reproducible review protocol.
Evaluate compatibility and bias before pooling.
Interpret heterogeneity and limits of generalization.

lesson.overview: A systematic review defines a question, search strategy, eligibility criteria and appraisal process before selecting evidence. Meta-analysis combines compatible estimates while representing uncertainty and heterogeneity; it does not make weak studies strong merely by averaging them. Outcome definitions, follow-up times, dependent estimates and implementation differences influence what can be combined. Publication and reporting biases can distort the available evidence. A graduate synthesis distinguishes the average effect from variation across settings and explains which decisions the evidence can reasonably inform.
lesson.worked_example: A review finds ten tutoring studies, but some report immediate arithmetic recall and others year-end problem solving. Combining all scores without examining constructs and follow-up would obscure the question. The review groups compatible outcomes and explains remaining heterogeneity.
lesson.activity: Write a review protocol on a specific teaching intervention. Define population, comparison, outcomes and timing; draft search terms and inclusion rules; design a risk-of-bias table; and critique whether a pooled effect would be meaningful.
lesson.reflection: When would a careful narrative synthesis be more honest than a single pooled number?

quiz.prompt: Eligibility criteria should be specified?
quiz.explain: Advance criteria reduce selective inclusion.

quiz.prompt: Pooling biased studies automatically removes bias?
quiz.explain: A precise average can preserve shared biases.

quiz.prompt: A review finds different effects across studies. What needs explanation?
choices: Variation in effects and study features
quiz.answer: Variation in effects and study features
quiz.explain: Differences across studies require substantive and statistical interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Multiple outcomes from the same study may be?
quiz.explain: Shared samples can correlate effect estimates.

quiz.prompt: Publication bias can occur when?
quiz.explain: Selective dissemination changes the observed evidence base.

quiz.prompt: A review protocol improves?
quiz.explain: Readers can inspect planned decisions and deviations.

quiz.prompt: A review combines immediate recall and year-long retention as one outcome. First examine?
choices: Growth in the total citation count
quiz.explain: Pooling requires a defensible common question.

quiz.prompt: A large pooled sample comes mostly from weak designs. The conclusion should?
choices: Use sample size as a cure for bias
quiz.explain: Precision and design validity are separate.

quiz.prompt: A search includes published papers but omits registered unpublished trials. This may miss?
choices: A guaranteed set of positive effects
A complete set of unbiased studies
quiz.explain: Unavailable or unpublished results can alter the evidence base.

quiz.prompt: Two reviewers disagree about inclusion. A protocol should provide?
quiz.explain: Transparent procedures improve reproducibility and reduce arbitrary selection.

quiz.prompt: A review pools immediate recall and year-long reasoning scores from studies with uneven reporting. Explain what should happen before a pooled conclusion.
quiz.answer: Assess outcome compatibility and timing, appraise risk of bias and investigate selective reporting. Explain heterogeneity and use separate or narrative synthesis if one pooled effect would obscure the question.
quiz.explain: Assess outcome compatibility and timing, appraise risk of bias and investigate selective reporting. Explain heterogeneity and use separate or narrative synthesis if one pooled effect would obscure the question.

nodes.title: Learning Design Research and Graduate Capstone
nodes.goal: Iteratively develop and evaluate an educational intervention with a defensible theory of change.
learning_outcomes: Connect theory to specific design features.
Document and interpret iterative changes.
State bounded design principles and transfer conditions.

lesson.overview: Design-based research develops an intervention while studying how learning works in a real context. Iterative cycles connect a conjecture, designed features, observed processes and revisions. Iteration creates useful local knowledge but complicates causal attribution when many features change together. Graduate work therefore documents versions, explains why changes were made and separates evidence of usability from evidence of learning. A capstone contributes a bounded design principle, examines equity and implementation, and proposes further tests rather than claiming a universal solution from one site.
lesson.worked_example: A team expects comparison prompts to improve fraction explanations. In one cycle, learners misunderstand the prompt wording; in the next, wording changes while the comparison task stays constant. The record separates improved usability from later evidence about conceptual learning.
lesson.activity: Produce a graduate design dossier: theoretical conjecture, prototype lesson, observation plan, two planned iterations, version log, learning measure and equity critique. State a rival explanation and a follow-up study capable of challenging the proposed design principle.
lesson.reflection: What evidence would justify transferring your design to a different age group or setting?

quiz.prompt: A conjecture map links?
quiz.explain: The map makes the proposed mechanism explicit.

quiz.prompt: Changing many features at once makes it harder to?
quiz.explain: Multiple simultaneous changes complicate causal interpretation.

quiz.prompt: High satisfaction with a prototype establishes?
quiz.explain: Enjoyment and learning are distinct outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A version log is useful because it?
choices: Links evidence to the tested version
quiz.answer: Links evidence to the tested version
quiz.explain: Documented changes make iterative research interpretable.

quiz.prompt: A design principle from one site should be?
choices: Bounded by context and further tests
quiz.answer: Bounded by context and further tests
quiz.explain: Transfer requires evidence about relevant conditions.

quiz.prompt: A strong graduate capstone contributes?
choices: An evidenced design claim with limits
quiz.answer: An evidenced design claim with limits
quiz.explain: The contribution connects theory, design and critical evidence.

quiz.prompt: A prototype improves navigation but learning scores remain unchanged. Claim?
choices: Complete disproof of the design theory
quiz.explain: Evidence should be separated by the outcome measured.

quiz.prompt: A design claim depends on small-group dialogue. A transfer study in large lectures should examine?
choices: Whether dialogue can be assumed stable
quiz.explain: Transfer depends on preserving or adapting relevant mechanisms.

quiz.prompt: A second cycle changes prompts, tasks and feedback. Attribution should be?
quiz.explain: Bundled revisions prevent isolating one contribution.

quiz.prompt: A capstone reports only successful iterations. What is lost?
choices: The existence of the final prototype
quiz.explain: Unsuccessful cycles can reveal constraints and explain design decisions.

quiz.prompt: A prototype becomes easier to use after several simultaneous changes, but learning gains are unclear. Frame an appropriate graduate design claim.
quiz.answer: Claim improved usability for the tested version, not established learning gains. Document the changes, measure learning separately and test the proposed mechanism in a further iteration with bounded transfer claims.
quiz.explain: Claim improved usability for the tested version, not established learning gains. Document the changes, measure learning separately and test the proposed mechanism in a further iteration with bounded transfer claims.
